title: Fiance of man shot by police questions why officer used lethal force
subtitle: The fiance of a man shot and killed by a Regina police officer has taken to social media to express her belief that he did not have to die.
article: As the family of a 41-year-old man shot and killed by a Regina police officer takes to social media to question the use of lethal force, scrutiny of the impending police investigation into the death is just beginning.

"Whenever something like this happens, Section 91.1 of the Police Act specifies that an independent investigation observer is assigned by the Ministry of Justice," Drew Wilby, a spokesman with the Ministry of Justice, explained in an interview Monday. "We have done that."

A former Saskatchewan RCMP officer who has no employment history with the Regina Police Service (RPS) has been assigned to observe the investigation, ensuring it meets investigative standards and follows the proper processes.
At the end of the investigation, the observer will provide a report to the deputy minister of justice, and the ministry will determine whether the investigation was conducted appropriately.
"The police are competent in what they do," said Wilby. "We have full confidence in their ability to conduct an independent investigation and take a look at the circumstances of what happened."
Generally, in the case of a police-involved fatality, the Saskatchewan Coroners Service also calls an inquest.

Although the RPS has not yet officially released the man's name, family on social media have identified him as Geoff Morris. Police say he was killed during an alleged hostage situation Saturday morning.
In a Facebook post published on the night of May 4, the same day Morris was killed, a woman identifying herself as Morris' fiancee wrote extensively about the moments leading up his death.
"Honestly it wasn't necessary for them to kill him, they could've just tased him," wrote Jasmine Brass, who said she was present when Morris was killed.
She described Morris as someone struggling with mental health issues. "I'm so broken right now, but deep deep down I'm at peace for him to be free of his lifetime of abuse and depression," she wrote.

According to police, officers responded just after 5:30 a.m. Saturday to an apartment in the 1900 block of Halifax Street after receiving reports of a disturbance. Police on scene reported finding a man with a knife holding a hostage. Morris was shot later that morning.
Speaking at an unrelated news conference Monday, Regina police Chief Evan Bray briefly addressed reporters' questions about the controversy now swirling on social media.
"I am aware of lots of social media dialogue. I'm aware of where the investigation is at, but really at this point I'm not in a position where I can offer any further comment," he said.

Questioned further, Bray said, "I gave a fairly lengthy press conference the other day on the issue. There's lots that could be said, but I want the process to unfold naturally, and so today I'm not going to focus on that, and I respectfully ask you to respect that."
Wilby noted that anyone concerned about the investigation or the acts of an officer can file a complaint to the Public Complaints Commission, which is a civilian-led oversight body.

"They (police-involved shootings) don't happen very often, which is good, but when they do we have a process that's in place to ensure that things are followed, and to make sure that there's transparency with the ministry," said Wilby.

In 50 years, Regina police officers have been involved in six previous shootings that resulted in a death: a 16-year-old Regina boy in 1998 who was armed with a hunting knife; a 20-year-old woman armed with a pistol in 1996; a 26-year-old man armed with a knife during a domestic dispute in 1993; a 17-year-old boy who shot himself with a high-powered rifle after he was shot in the hand by police in 1989; a 38-year-old gun-toting man who had written a suicide note before confronting police in 1984; and a 19-year-old man in 1969 during a police stake-out.

At a news conference on Saturday, Bray said officers were on scene for an hour trying to de-escalate the situation. A request was made for more resources, including crisis negotiators, SWAT and EMS, and members of these groups were on scene when the gun was fired.

"Ultimately an officer made a decision to discharge a firearm as an acceptable level of force to stop a situation because of a fear he had that someone else could be seriously injured," he said, adding that he could not clarify whether the officer feared for the safety of another officer or a civilian.

In her post, Brass wrote that she and her sister were trying to calm Morris early Saturday morning, and it felt like "hours" before a negotiator arrived. She believes Morris became more agitated afterward.

Also taking to social media was Dakota Morris, who wrote, "The cops didn't just take away someones life that morning, they took away my dads. Anyone who knows him knows was the type of person to give the shirt off his back. He was one of a kind and didn't deserve what happened to him." She called for better police training regarding those struggling with mental health issues.

"He wasn't the monster that they're making him out to be. He loved his fiancée more then Ive ever seen him love anyone. That was his rock and his home, they took away someone who was struggling with ptsd and depression," Dakota said, also questioning the level of experience of the officer involved.
Police have neither publicly identified the shooter, nor the officer's years of service.

"Even though we train for it, even though it's something that officers right from recruit training step out on the street and they understand they might be confronted with it, this is not an easy day for officers," said Bray.
Officers attended to the same Halifax Street residence on March 13 as part of what police described in a news release an ongoing investigation involving the RPS's Street Gang Unit into weapons.

At that time, Morris, along with a 19-year-old man, were arrested at the residence and charged with possession of methamphetamine. Morris was released and due to appear in Regina court April 29 on that and a separate charge of evading police, stemming from Jan. 18 when it's alleged he failed to stop his vehicle for police. A co-accused appeared in court on his behalf last week and indicated Morris was ill on that day.
According to court documents, Morris's listed address was a suite at 1927 Halifax St., where he was killed Saturday.
The Leader-Post reached out to family members for an interview, but no one had responded as of late Monday afternoon.
